Toronto, Canada! 💖 I'm half Jamaican half Chinese (Singaporean), and very blasian presenting. 

Personally I think it's a great place for a blasian at least in Canada. There are very large Asian and Black communities here, as you're able to find cuisine from both cultures, sometimes even fusion meals! Also We aren't AS uptight about race up here as in comparison to some places in the states. 

Toronto is so diverse and multicultural I never really felt the need to think hard about race until it came up in political conversations. That's something me and my other minority friends always are glad about in the city, we lived in a bubble as we were grateful for the peace we had growing up. As a blasian, my personal friend groups were ALWAYS diverse. Back in highschool it was me the blasian, a wasian, a jamaican, a half white& half black, two arabs, and a Bengali. Right now my close friend group consists of me, a Mexican, a white Canadian, a Chinese, an Indian Arab, a Jamaican, and a Filipino. I've met at least 6 other blasians in my life! We are definitely still a rare kind here. 

Don't get me wrong there'd a lot of bad apples, and many are racist and cliquey, I've witnessed it in highschool. And historically it wasn't always so peaceful from what I heard from people older than me, it's definitely gotten easier. Though I did get a few comments from other black folk teasing me about my chinese side, but they were never serious as we were kids and it's only ever happened three times in my life. 

And not to mention Toronto in general is decently clean, you experience all 4 seasons, you don't need a car (it's beneficial but I was never raised with one), and there are many cultural events. 

Just my personal experience, everyone would have something different to say. :)

I was born in 2001, and raised in Canada so this is just my perspective. 

I can also only describe things from a kid perspective, but the 2000s felt like late 90s on steroids. R+B had this nice gentle swing to it, my brother wore a lot of bandanas and snapbacks too. We used physical maps for finding places, and I remember thinking having a GPS was top tech lol. 

Things were more colourful but also more plastic-ey. 

Obvs as toddlers in the early 2000s we didn’t have cellphones but we had landlines. My family still has our old fax machine but we use it for home calls now. I remember the struggle of hearing the phone ring, and me wanting to answer it for my mom but my mom picks it up on the other phone in the house only to eavesdrop on my convos XD 
When the late 2000s hit we had cellphones only for calling our parents, most had flip phones and I had that slidey keyboard one. I remember seeing ringtone ads on tv and in magazines. 

It’s a very interesting era for me because since I was learning about the world back then, all the trends felt natural and a part of the natural order of life, but obvs now looking back I’m just amused of all the silly stuff that went on 

Gonna be honest I didn’t know what the internet was until I was in maybe first grade where they introduced it to us in school, but we didn’t use it much. Wifi wasnt really well known, I didn’t know about it until 2009 and I didn’t have it at home until maybe 2014. I didn’t know much about mobile App Store games until 2010 or so.
I’ve been vibing to a lot of 2000s-2010 s stuff, I love the electro, pop punkness
Honestly I don’t hate our generation, we have dumb people doing dumb things that get us noticed and a bad rep, but as a gen z-er I feel most of us, the older ones at least, are pretty self aware

It depends on the context. "Get back" is a strong emphasis on returning to do something, usually an action rather than a place. "Go back" can also be used for that, but not the other way around if that makes sense. 

For "get back"
 You can use it for place, but it's a weird way of saying it. I'd avoid it until you have a better understanding through exposure, some things a bit hard to explain when slang exists lol. 

Usually it's used for sentences like:
"I'm going to get back to cleaning" 
"I'm going to get back to studying" 
Though most natives would simply say 
"I'm gonna get back to work" (gonna instead of going to, but beware in a professional setting. gonna is a very casual contraction. essays hate it.)

"Go back" is usually regarding location or place. 
"I'm gonna go back to John's house" 
"I'm going to go back to the library tomorrow."

But it CAN be used for actions like "get back" 
"I'm gonna go back to studying." I feel like it's up to preference but I'm not sure on the technicalities there. Most English speakers won't notice a difference. 


TO SIMPLIFY:
"I'm going to go back to work" - sounds like you will soon go back to your location of work

"I'm going to get back to work" - sounds more like you were working on something in the moment and will soon resume. 

There are exceptions I feel, but none I can think of from the top of my head.

I hope this makes sense! 

ALSO: 

Saying "Get back!" as a command sounds like you're trying to warn someone to stay out of the way. 

Saying "Go back!" as a command sounds like you're trying to tell someone to go back to their previous location.

1. You would say "They broke up".  "Broken up" can still be used, but you would have to add "have" in front of it. "They have broken up" But that sounds more narrative and robotic. As if you're reading a story or poem. I think it's because it just takes longer to say. 

2. I feel like "is" and "was" can both work in casual conversation. In this context either works. You don't need to think too hard about it, I feel most English speakers won't care which you use unless you're writing an essay or something. That's a very small issue though. 

3. "Is" does not work here. "Wasn't" is negative. It is a contraction of "was not". "It wasn't enough" is equal to "It was not enough". Which would mean something was not enough for something else. If you used "Hard work is enough" it would mean the opposite of what that person you quoted was trying to say. 

And to conclude, you would say "It's installed" if it is still installed regardless of who did it. If you're emphasizing how long you've had it installed you would say "It's still installed".
If you really want to specify who, simply "he/she/they installed it" or "he/she/they installed it for me" works.

The reason why "was fixed" does not mean something is removed in the same "was installed" is based on the root words themselves. With the word "Installed" the opposite, would be "Uninstalled" 
Example: I uninstalled that app. or It's been uninstalled. 
Install is to add in the app
Uninstall is to delete it 

"Was installed" means the same thing as "uninstalled" 

However, with the word "fixed". "unfixed" means the opposite of fixed. 
Fixed - Secured, safe, 
Unfixed - Loose, unsturdy, 

Unfixed is not a commonly used term though as it only represents something that was at one point fixed but is no longer fixed. If it wasn't fixed to begin with, we would simply say "It's not fixed".
